q: White phosphorus bursts into flames when exposed to air. (2024)
e: White phosphorus is extremely reactive and spontaneously ignites in air.

q: Reactant particles moving in random directions possess kinetic energy. (2024)
e: Particles in motion possess kinetic energy.

q: A rate is always expressed as a positive quantity. (2024)
e: By convention, reaction rate is always expressed as a positive quantity.

q: Transition state is a highly energetic state that would be highly unstable. (2025)
e: The transition state is a short-lived intermediate with high potential energy and extreme instability.

q: The name of theory that is used to explain the rate of reaction is collision theory. (2026)
e: Collision theory is used to explain how chemical reactions occur and why reaction rates differ.

q: All collisions between reactant particles result in the formation of reaction products. (2025)
e: Only effective collisions with sufficient activation energy and correct orientation form products.

q: The rate of a reaction depends on the enthalpy of the reaction. (2024)
e: The rate of reaction depends on factors such as activation energy, temperature, and concentration, not enthalpy change.

q: An iron nail reacts rapidly in the air as it rusts. (2025)
e: Rusting of iron is a slow chemical reaction.

q: Transition state is a highly energetic state that would be highly stable. (2025)
e: The transition state is highly unstable due to its high energy content.

q: The unit for the rate of a chemical reaction in solution is mol dm^-3 s^-1. (2025)
e: The rate of reaction in solution measures concentration change per unit time (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹).

q: The catalysts provide an alternative pathway for the reaction with lower activation energy. (2025)
e: Catalysts speed up reactions by offering a mechanism with lower activation energy.

q: If there are the more successful collisions, the more activated complex leads to the rate of a reaction being faster. (2026)
e: A higher frequency of successful collisions leads to a faster reaction rate.

q: Large pieces of wood are difficult to ignite whereas small pieces burn more rapidly. (2024)
e: Smaller pieces have a larger surface area exposed to oxygen, resulting in a faster rate of reaction.

q: The rate of a reaction depends on the rate of successful collisions between reactant particles. (2024)
e: Reaction rate directly depends on how frequently effective collisions occur.

q: When the particles collide with the incorrect orientation, they must have enough energy for a successful collision to produce a reaction. (2025)
e: Collisions with incorrect orientation are unsuccessful regardless of the amount of energy.

q: Pressure changes do not markedly affect the solid or liquid phases. (2024)
e: Solids and liquids are virtually incompressible, so pressure changes have little to no effect.

q: The rate of reaction is proportional to the time taken. (2025)
e: The rate of reaction is inversely proportional to the time taken.

q: The unsuccessful collisions with insufficient energy do not produce a reaction. (2026)
e: Collisions lacking the required activation energy fail to form products.

q: The unsuccessful collisions with sufficient energy do not produce a reaction. (2025)
e: Even with sufficient energy, collisions fail to produce a reaction if the orientation is incorrect.

q: If the colliding particles have the correct orientation, they will bounce off each other. (2025)
e: Particles with correct orientation and sufficient energy will form products rather than bounce off.

q: The unit for the rate of a chemical reaction in solution is mol dm^-3 s^-1. (2026)
e: The standard unit for reaction rate in solution is mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

q: Platinum is used as a catalyst in the lead chamber process. (2026)
e: Nitric oxide (NO) is used as the catalyst in the lead chamber process, whereas platinum is used in the contact process.

q: The reaction time is directly proportional to the rate. (2026)
e: Reaction time is inversely proportional to the rate of reaction.
